summary: Explains issues with sending RTP data packets and RTCP control packets on a single UDP port, and says when it is and is not appropriate. It updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 and describes how SDP can signal it. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: RTP carries media data, while RTCP carries control information about an RTP session. RFC 5761 explains how both can use one UDP port and which packet values and signaling rules keep them distinguishable.

questions: can rtp and rtcp use the same port
how to multiplex rtp and rtcp
how to tell rtp from rtcp packets
which rtp payload types are blocked when multiplexing
subtitle: How RTP data and RTCP control packets can share one UDP port, and the restrictions that make this possible.

tldr.problem: RTP data and RTCP control traffic historically use separate UDP ports. Network Address Port Translation and firewalls can make managing both ports more difficult.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5761 permits both packet types on one port when the payload type and RTCP packet-type fields distinguish them. SDP uses the media-level a=rtcp-mux attribute to signal multiplexing.
tldr.outcome: The RFC says multiplexing is acceptable for signaled unicast sessions, SHOULD NOT be used for Any Source Multicast, and MAY be used for specified Source-Specific Multicast flows. It updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551 and has later updates of its own.

today: RFC 5761 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3550 and RFC 3551. It has been updated by RFC 8035 and RFC 8858.

sections.title: Why Share RTP and RTCP Ports
sections.content:
The Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) carries data, and its associated control protocol, RTCP, carries control information. They have historically used separate UDP ports. The RFC notes that maintaining multiple Network Address Port Translation (NAPT) bindings can be costly and that firewalls may need multiple ports opened.

RFC 5761 describes sending RTP and RTCP for one media type on a single port. It does not cover multiplexing multiple media types, such as audio and video, on one port. The change shifts packet separation into the RTP implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: Using one port can reduce the number of network bindings and firewall openings needed for a session. The RTP implementation must then distinguish data packets from control packets itself.

sections.title: Why RTP Originally Used Separate Ports
sections.content:
Separate ports let the transport layer distinguish data from control packets. The RFC lists simplicity and efficiency as reasons for that choice: RTP software did not need to separate the packet kinds, and demultiplexing could happen in one place.

A separate RTCP multicast group and port can also let third-party monitors observe reception-quality information without receiving data packets. These reasons remain useful in many settings, but separate ports can complicate NAT traversal and firewall administration.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate ports make packet sorting simpler and let a monitor receive RTCP without media data. Sharing a port can help with NAT and firewall configuration, but moves packet sorting into RTP software.

sections.title: Distinguishing the Two Packet Types
sections.content:
On a shared port, the RTCP packet-type field occupies the same position as the RTP marker bit combined with the RTP payload type. Receivers can distinguish the packet kinds only if the RTP payload types do not conflict with RTCP packet types, and a payload type plus 128 also does not conflict with an RTCP type when the RTP marker bit is set.

For multiplexed sessions, RTP payload types 64 through 95 MUST NOT be used. Dynamic payload types SHOULD be chosen from 96 through 127 where possible. Values below 64 MAY be used if needed, preferring values not statically assigned by the RTP profile.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver examines a field shared by the two packet formats to decide whether a packet is RTP or RTCP. Some RTP payload numbers are therefore reserved from use in a multiplexed session.

sections.title: Signaling Multiplexing with SDP
sections.content:
When Session Description Protocol (SDP) offer/answer is used, the media-level a=rtcp-mux attribute requests RTP and RTCP on one port. The offer MUST include the attribute to request multiplexing, and an answerer that agrees MUST include it in its answer.

If the answer does not include the attribute, the offerer MUST NOT multiplex and instead uses a separate RTCP port. In declarative SDP, the attribute means the sender will multiplex, and the receiver MUST be ready to receive RTCP on the RTP port. ICE and SIP forking can require additional candidates or listening on both ports.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides must agree to share the port in SDP. If the answer does not include the attribute, the session uses separate RTP and RTCP ports.

sections.title: Where Multiplexing Is Appropriate
sections.content:
For unicast, multiplexing is acceptable when the payload-type restrictions are followed and the choice is signaled in advance. For Any Source Multicast (ASM), RTP and RTCP SHOULD NOT be multiplexed; the RFC cites the smaller NAT concern and the value of separate ports for third-party RTCP-only monitors.

For Source-Specific Multicast (SSM), the guidance depends on the flow. RTP and RTCP between a media sender and distribution source MAY share a port when properly signaled. The distribution source MAY also multiplex traffic toward receivers, though this may hinder third-party monitoring. The receiver-to-source path carries RTCP only.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC treats unicast as a suitable case when both sides signal the change and follow the packet rules. It recommends separate ports for Any Source Multicast and gives narrower permission for SSM flows.

sections.title: Bandwidth, Compression, and Security
sections.content:
When quality-of-service systems classify by the shared port, RTCP joins the RTP flow. The reservation therefore needs to include RTCP bandwidth. In the usual case, RTCP is limited to 5% of the RTP session bandwidth, and a reservation SHOULD be 105% of the SDP b=AS: value.

Mixing RTCP packets into an RTP stream can disrupt header-compression patterns, especially when a classifier considers only IP addresses and UDP ports. The RFC says this effect should be considered in systems that rely on compression.

The RFC does not believe multiplexing adds new security considerations. With Secure RTP (SRTP), multiplexing MUST happen below the SRTP layer: the sender creates SRTP and SRTCP packets with their separate cryptographic contexts, then places them on one port.
sections.plainLanguage: One shared flow needs enough reserved bandwidth for both media and control packets. Security processing still uses separate RTP and RTCP contexts before the packets are combined for transport.

cells: Acceptable when signaled and payload-type rules are followed
MAY multiplex on specified flows when signaled
